newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel halts talks, may re-enter Palestinian areas.
newsitem.headline: Israel halts talks, may re-enter Palestinian areas.

text.p: Israel suspended peace talks over a deadly suicide attack, made arrests and threatened to re-enter Palestinian areas to seize "terrorists" on Thursday if President Yasser Arafat's forces failed to do the job.

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's cabinet demanded Arafat act against Moslem militants responsible for the double suicide attack that killed 13 people and wounded 170 at a Jewish market in Jerusalem on Wednesday.

"The cabinet decision is quite clear. If Israel has to, that is if the Palestinian Authority is not going to do what it is supposed to do against the terrorists, Israel will have to do it," Netanyahu's adviser David Bar-Illan told Reuters.

"Israel will have to go into the areas controlled by the Palestinian Authority if that is necessary and get the terrorists there," he said. A leaflet issued in the name of the Moslem militant Hamas group claimed responsibility.

Israeli security forces raided several West Bank villages and arrested Hamas activists and their families. Late on Wednesday, Netanyahu's security cabinet ordered a halt to peace talks and vowed to act.

Palestinians said soldiers stormed Dahariyeh village near Hebron and arrested members of two families whose sons, both Islamic militants, have been missing for 15 months. It was not immediately clear if the missing pair were the bombers.

"The meaning of the decisions last night is that Israel is going to apply various types of pressures on Arafat to create for him an incentive to act against the terror," said Shimon Shiffer, diplomatic correspondent of the daily Yedioth Ahronoth.

He predicted Israel would arrest Hamas and Islamic Jihad activists in areas under its security control, jam Palestinian radio and television stations, freeze Palestinian accounts in Israel and urge Washington to hold up economic aid to Arafat.

Israel has only rarely re-entered the self-rule areas of Gaza and the West Bank to make arrests or battle Palestinians. It has handed the areas over to Palestinian self-rule under peace deals signed since 1993.

Israel sealed off the West Bank and Gaza Strip immediately after the attack. Military checkpoints blocked movements of residents and tourists alike. Police ordered shut a welfare office which Israeli sources said was illegally operating on behalf of the Palestinian Authority in Arab East Jerusalem.

A Palestinian security official said Arafat, who condemned the bombing, had declared a state of emergency in Palestinian areas and ordered the arrest of activists of "extremist groups" including Hamas and Islamic Jihad.

Arafat's adviser Nabil Abu Rdainah insisted the Palestinian Authority was preventing attacks from being launched from areas under its control and warned Israel it would be "overstepping the red line" by entering Palestinian-controlled areas.

"The Israeli government would be fully responsible for the consequences of such acts," he said without elaborating. PLO officials said police were under orders from Arafat to prevent re-entry of Israeli soldiers into self-rule areas.

Nearly a full day after the mid-day blasts, police were still trying to identify some of the bodies blown apart by the two 10-kg (22 pound) bombs that the well-dressed attackers carried in briefcases.
Police urged the public to be on the alert for suspicious people and objects. Suicide bombers killed 59 people in a wave of attacks over eight days in February and March 1996.
Public Security Minister Avigdor Kahalani said there were signs the explosives might have been assembled in a bomb laboratory uncovered by Palestinian police in June near Bethlehem in the West Bank.
At the Jerusalem market, stalls reopened for business after municipal workers spent the night removing debris and cleaning.

World leaders urged Israel and the Palestinians to press on with negotiations but U.S. special Middle East envoy Dennis Ross postponed a planned mission to salvage peacemaking during a period of national mourning.
U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright said she was working to renew U.S. aid to Palestinians despite the bombing.
The law making it possible for the United States to give aid to Arafat's Palestinian Authority expires on August 12 and there has been doubt about whether Congress will extend it.
